title: There is a soft bigotry of low expectations but there is soft bigotry of high expectations, too.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: A summer-series post that begins with a disagreement with his psychotherapist daughter about the phrase getting better. Skelton concludes that in learning, getting better is a continuum with no end point rather than a state of being well again. He then takes the phrase soft bigotry of low expectations and extends it beyond disadvantaged groups to comfortable schools that coast on easily met targets. His twist is that the slogan you can be whatever you want to be is its own soft bigotry, because it sets up false futures and eventual frustration. The remedy he proposes is targets that sit just beyond current reach but are attainable, reset after each success, and offered to students, teachers and schools alike.
points: Getting better in learning is an ongoing continuum rather than an end point at which a person is finished.
Low expectations are not confined to disadvantaged groups; coasting schools that settle for easily met targets practise the same bigotry.
Telling young people they can be anything they want is untrue and can produce frustration and a sense of failure.
The practical answer is a moving target that is always just out of reach yet achievable, reset after reflection each time it is met.
quotes: Getting better in learning isn’t reaching an end point where we are ‘better’ now. It’s a continuum along which we learn and improve in some way.

I don’t think that the ‘slow bigotry of low expectations’ is restricted only to disadvantaged groups. I’ve been in lots of definitely not disadvantaged schools and classrooms where there are low expectations, too.

Comfortable in the knowledge that most targets will be achieved by most students, these schools and teachers settle for not much more than that. It is these schools and classrooms that the word ‘coasting’ often describes.
I’ve heard two or three times this week the sentence ‘You can be whatever you want to be’. It’s well meant and might help some of us push ourselves a little bit harder. But it is also simply untrue.

You can be whatever you want to be’ tells me that there is soft bigotry in high expectations, too. Creating expectations of a false future for people will, for many of those people, only bring frustration and a sense of failure.

We need to set targets for our students and ourselves that are, right now, just out of our grasp but reachable. And each time they are reached we can, after reflection with and about our students’ capabilities, reset them again to be just out of reach but achievable again.
